pack.title: Gráinne Ní Mháille: Clew Bay, London, and return

presentation.anchor: Gráinne Ní Mháille · Clew Bay · Rockfleet · the 1593 papers
presentation.question: Can she preserve her family, authority, and way of life as Tudor power closes around Clew Bay?
presentation.opening: Nine chapters follow the system that formed Gráinne's power, the pressure that broke its local answers, the 1593 journey into English administration, and the unfinished return to Mayo.
presentation.evidenceLimit: The county account joins coast, place records, petitions, interrogatory answers, official correspondence, and later reception. It does not invent private scenes, a Greenwich conversation, or certainty where the surviving accounts conflict.
presentation.sourceTitle: The 1593 petition, SP 63/170 interrogatory and answers, and the September royal draft
presentation.sourceDetail: Claims C01–C16 · C17 remains excluded or reception-only and C18 is excluded as a period title · targeted expanded-story review remains open for Chapters 2 and 4 and historian confirmation of the C04 citation
presentation.artifactPrompt: Trace Clew Bay to London and back, keeping the documentary record beside the later stories.
presentation.tegCanDo: Recognise and produce supported Irish for place, family, movement, asking, answering, and return inside a historical account.

chapters.title: An Bá is an Umhaill · Clew Bay and Umhaill

pages.title: A coast that faces the open sea
pages.body: Mayo's western edge opens onto the farraige — the sea. Here the water is not a border at the end of the land. It is the road, the larder and the source of power. To understand Gráinne Ní Mháille, begin with the sea her people worked.
pages.detail: The chapter opens on the water because the sea, not the shore, explains the kind of authority this coast could hold.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of Clew Bay · not documentary evidence

pages.title: One bay, many islands
pages.body: Clew Bay — an bá — is a wide inlet studded with islands and sheltered by headlands. A bay like this is a system: safe water, landing places, and routes out to the open Atlantic. It gathers boats the way a marketplace gathers people.
pages.detail: A named bay is a named place of power. Whoever controls its water controls who moves through it.

pages.title: The islands were homes, not scenery
pages.context: Clare Island · Achill · the inner isles
pages.body: Clare Island guards the bay mouth; Achill rises to the north; smaller islands fill the inner water. People lived, farmed and fished across them. A leader who could move freely between them held something a land-bound lord could not.
pages.detail: This is landscape as infrastructure. The islands are the reason sea power here was worth having.

pages.title: This coast is a particular place
pages.body: The territory around the bay had a name: Umhaill, the Owles. It was a specific áit — a place — with its own people, boundaries and loyalties. Naming it matters: the story is not about a coast in general but about this one, and who held it.
pages.detail: Áit is a small word doing heavy work. A place with a name is a place worth keeping or taking.

pages.title: A polity that lived by the sea
pages.body: The Uí Mháille (O'Malleys) drew their living from the water: fishing, trade, tolls on those who passed, and — when it served — seizure. This was a normal Atlantic lordship, not a lawless free sea. Its wealth and its risks both came in by boat.
pages.detail: Say it plainly: maintenance by land and sea included tolling and taking, alongside trade. Sanitising it into pure commerce would falsify the record.

pages.title: Saying where you are from
pages.body: In Irish you can place yourself with a small frame: as, meaning 'from'. Is as Maigh Eo mé — I am from Mayo. Gráinne's world begins with origin: which coast, which people, which bay you belong to.
pages.detail: You will reuse this frame later, when Gráinne must give her own name and origin to the English state.

pages.title: An outsider names her power
pages.body: Years before the 1593 crisis, the Lord Deputy Sir Henry Sidney later wrote that he had met a notable sea captain from this coast — a woman with galleys and fighting men. The recognition comes from an English official, in his words, but it tells us her maritime power was real enough for the state to notice.
pages.detail: Sidney wrote the memoir for Sir Francis Walsingham on 1 March 1582/3, recalling a Galway meeting during his 1576 deputyship. Carew MS 601 and TNA SP 12/159 preserve the candidate citation trail; the folio and diplomatic wording still require historian confirmation.

exercise.hint: Replay the words. Farraige is the open water; bá is the sheltered inlet; áit is the named coast.
exercise.recovery: Those two do not belong together. Keep the first word selected and try another meaning.

pages.title: What the coast can and cannot tell us
pages.body: The geography is real and the recognition of her sea power is well attested. But a coastline cannot, by itself, narrate a life. What the bay supports is the shape of a world; the people who moved through it must be read from the surviving record.
pages.detail: Holding this limit makes the story sturdier: we claim a maritime world the evidence supports, not a scene we cannot see.

pages.title: The sea makes a leader — but not alone
pages.body: Clew Bay could make a leader who lived by boats. But sea power on its own is fragile. It has to rest on people: marriages, children and followers who make a coast into a household you can defend. That is where the story turns next.
pages.detail: The chapter exits with a question, not a word list: what holds this sea power together when the water alone is not enough?

chapters.title: Cleamhnas is Gaol · Marriage, kin, and alliances
chapters.place: Umhaill · the families around Clew Bay

pages.title: Sea power had to rest on people
pages.body: Boats could move authority across Clew Bay, but they could not hold it alone. Gráinne's teaghlach — her family and household — linked people, land, boats and obligations. In this world, kinship was not background to power. It was one of the ways power endured.
pages.detail: The papers let us see named relationships and political stakes. They do not let us invent a private family scene.

pages.title: Marriage joined houses and territories
pages.body: The 1593 answers record Gráinne's marriages — first to an O'Flaherty leader the papers call Donall Ichoggy (modern Irish: Dónal an Chogaidh Ó Flaithbheartaigh), and later to Risdeárd an Iarainn Bourke. Those marriages connected her to two powerful Connacht families. The broad sequence is supportable; exact wedding years and the later stories attached to the marriages are not equally secure.
pages.detail: This chapter does not stage a battlement divorce or repeat the one-year-marriage tale as fact.

pages.title: The record names the people at stake
pages.context: Children and brother · named in the papers
pages.body: The surviving papers name sons who matter to the 1593 crisis, including Tibbott, and they name her deartháir — her brother Donal. A mac is a son; a deartháir is a brother. These are not labels in a family tree. Later, the state will use these relationships as leverage.
pages.detail: The wider family can be explored in closer detail, but the main path keeps only the relationships that change the crisis.

pages.title: A woman recognised as a political actor
pages.body: Bean means woman. Here it names a fact the English record itself could not ignore: Gráinne was a woman exercising maritime and political authority in a world whose officials usually wrote power in male terms. The word is not a diminishment. It sharpens what made their recognition unusual.
pages.detail: The chapter keeps gender visible without turning it into shame, novelty, or the modern title 'pirate queen.'

pages.title: Names are not a domestic scene
pages.body: The questions and answers preserve parents, marriages, children and political claims because the English state wanted to know what Gráinne held and who was connected to her. They do not preserve an ordinary evening, a private argument, or the texture of affection inside the household.
pages.detail: The evidence supports a family system with political force. It does not authorise us to make the family perform for the learner.

pages.title: The family needed a defensible base
pages.body: Kinship could connect authority across the coast, but people, boats and goods still needed a place to gather and endure. The story now narrows from the whole bay to one inlet and one caisleán at the tide line: Rockfleet.
pages.detail: The next chapter asks how one place could hold the family system without pretending the walls preserve a family tableau.

pages.title: A castle where the road is water
pages.body: At Rockfleet, the inlet comes close to the walls. A caisleán here is more than a building set beside a view: it stands where boats can arrive, shelter and leave again.
pages.detail: The chapter begins with geography because the water explains why the place could matter.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of Rockfleet at the tide line · not documentary evidence

pages.title: The tide changes the threshold
pages.body: The shore is not a fixed line. Water depth, wind and the turn of the tide change when a boat can approach and where it can wait. That makes local knowledge part of the stronghold.
pages.detail: A castle on this inlet cannot be understood as an isolated tower on dry land.

pages.title: Boats extend the walls across the bay
pages.body: The inlet gives the household a defended landing. The boats carry people, goods, news and force beyond it. Castle and fleet do different work, but each makes the other more useful.
pages.detail: That connection is the chapter's first change: Rockfleet becomes a system rather than a landmark.

pages.detail: The documents give these relationships political weight without giving us a private family portrait.

pages.title: Relationships were part of authority
pages.body: Rockfleet is associated with Gráinne's Bourke marriage and later base. Her authority also depended on relationships that reached beyond one household: followers, neighbouring powers and shifting alliances all mattered.
pages.detail: The surviving record is strongest when it names people inside a dispute. It is weaker as a window into ordinary domestic life.

pages.title: Harbour, household and stronghold worked together
pages.body: The landing makes movement possible. The walls protect a base. The household and followers turn that base into lived authority. Remove one part and the others become less secure.
pages.detail: This is an interpretation built from place, later association and the political relationships visible in the papers—not a recovered floor plan of Gráinne's daily life.

pages.title: The papers show a political household, not a private scene
pages.body: The State Papers name parents, marriages, children, lands and maintenance because those facts matter to a case before government. The questions shape what becomes visible.
pages.detail: A document made for state business cannot be treated as an intimate account simply because it names family relationships.

pages.detail: Keeping that limit visible makes the supported story stronger, not smaller.

pages.title: A connected system can be pressured at several points
pages.body: If boats are seized, movement narrows. If kin are held, the household is pressured. If maintenance is cut away, authority becomes harder to sustain. Rockfleet helps make the coming crisis legible.
pages.detail: The next chapter asks what road remains when local power can no longer resolve that pressure.

pages.title: The coast becomes a set of stakes
pages.body: Rockfleet has changed from a picturesque ruin into a place where movement, defence, family and livelihood meet. That makes the later losses concrete: pressure on the coast can reach every part of the system.
pages.detail: The chapter exits with a question rather than a vocabulary summary: what can Gráinne do when those connected supports are threatened together?

chapters.title: Cumhacht ar Muir · Power at sea
chapters.place: Clew Bay and the Atlantic routes

pages.title: A ship made the coast larger
pages.body: Long means ship. From Rockfleet, a ship could cross the bay, reach another harbour, carry goods, enforce a local claim on the water, or bring force where it was needed. Maritime authority was not a title held still on land. It moved.
pages.detail: This chapter keeps long as its only new headword and puts the earlier sea, bay and place words back to work.

pages.title: Maintenance came by land and sea
pages.body: In the 1593 answers, Gráinne described maintaining herself and her people by land and sea. That sentence joins livelihood to authority: boats supported a household, followers and political action. The claim comes through a petitioning voice, shaped to persuade, but it is still her account of how the system worked.
pages.detail: The record does not reduce her maritime life to one occupation. It presents a mixed economy of land, water, negotiation and force.

pages.title: Trade and tolls were parts of the same livelihood
pages.body: Goods moved through the bay and along the Atlantic coast. English observers and later historians describe trade and the taking of tolls on these routes; her own papers speak instead of maintenance by force, by land and sea. Neither activity was neutral: each depended on recognised local authority and on the ability to enforce it.
pages.detail: Calling the whole system trade would make it cleaner than the evidence allows; calling tolling her own self-description would blur unlike sources.

pages.title: The same reach could be used to take
pages.body: Her maintenance also included opportunistic seizure. English officials described that conduct as disorder and threat; her own account framed armed action as part of survival and service. The sources disagree in purpose, not merely in tone. The chapter keeps the taking visible without turning it into adventure.
pages.detail: The learner does not raid a ship or defeat an official. The action remains historical, consequential and outside the learner's role.

pages.title: Officials noticed a working force
pages.body: In a memoir written for Walsingham in 1582/3, Sidney recalled meeting Gráinne during his 1576 deputyship and linked her to galleys and fighting men. Later papers treat her maritime reach as something the state had to bargain with or suppress. This page keeps Sidney's reported numbers in the evidence detail rather than turning them into a counted muster.
pages.detail: Sidney reported her offer of three galleys and 200 fighting men. The candidate trail is Carew MS 601 and TNA SP 12/159, publicly cited at f. 27d; a historian must confirm that folio and the diplomatic wording before this beat joins the Learning spine or becomes release copy.

pages.title: A working system could also be broken
pages.context: From maritime reach to Bingham's pressure
pages.body: The sea system sustained people because ships, routes, kin and local authority reinforced one another. That also made it vulnerable. A governor who could imprison kin, seize leverage and deny maintenance did not need to win one dramatic battle. He could tighten every connection at once.
pages.detail: The next chapter follows that tightening as one movement rather than a year-by-year tour.

chapters.title: Bingham ag Teannadh · Bingham closes in

pages.title: The same coast now answered to a harder presidency
pages.body: Under Richard Bingham's presidency, the state pressed harder against local powers it regarded as disorderly or disloyal. For Gráinne, that pressure reached the long, the routes, the income and the people who made authority possible. The system built across the last chapters began to fail at several points at once.
pages.detail: This is not a contest between two equal character portraits. Bingham's office gave him prisons, officers and control over what counted as lawful force.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of Tudor coastal pressure · not documentary evidence

pages.title: Two accounts describe the same pressure differently
pages.body: Gráinne's case emphasised lost maintenance, seized goods and kin under threat. Bingham's letters cast her network as a source of disorder that demanded control. Each voice had a purpose. Reading them together reveals the conflict; it does not make every accusation on either side equally proven.
pages.detail: The bias is part of the evidence. It tells us what each writer needed the state to believe.

pages.title: A son and brother were held
pages.body: By 1593, her mac Tibbott was imprisoned under a treason charge and her deartháir Donal was also held. Caill means lose. The danger was no longer only lost income or a weakened fleet: she could lose the people named inside her political and family system.
pages.detail: The imprisonment is the tipping fact that makes London necessary. It is supported by the petition trail and the later royal draft.

pages.title: Without the fleet, the old answer weakened
pages.body: The petition presents her maintenance by land and sea as stripped away. Whether every disputed detail is accepted or not, the larger change is clear: the maritime leverage that had supported her household could no longer answer state pressure on its own.
pages.detail: The chapter does not turn a complex conflict into a single stolen-ship scene. The loss is systemic.

pages.title: One death remains a disputed edge
pages.body: Gráinne blamed Bingham's side for the death of her son Eóghan, recorded in English as Owen; the surviving accounts conflict over the circumstances. That accusation belongs in closer view because it deepens the stakes, but the main story does not pronounce a settled murder where the record does not support one.
pages.detail: The disagreement is consequential, so the uncertainty remains visible rather than being buried or dramatized.

pages.title: The coast could no longer solve the crisis
pages.body: Ships, kin and local bargaining had once given Gráinne several ways to act. By 1593, those answers were closing. Tibbott and Donal were held, maintenance was cut, and the governor controlled the machinery of force. The remaining route led outside Connacht: a petition to the Queen.
pages.detail: The next chapter begins with necessity, not pageantry. London matters because every local answer has narrowed.

chapters.title: An Bóthar go Londain · The road to London
chapters.place: Clew Bay · London · the Queen's process

pages.title: The petition became the remaining action
pages.context: July 1593 · a case addressed to power
pages.body: Iarr means ask. In 1593 Gráinne asked the Queen for enough maintenance to live on and for action concerning the pressure on her family. The petition also offered service against the Queen's enemies. It was a plea, a bargain and a crafted presentation of herself at once.
pages.detail: The language is courteous because the document needs to work. Courtesy does not make the stakes small.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of an Atlantic crossing · not a documentary voyage

pages.title: To ask was also to become legible to the state
pages.body: Her case translated a maritime life into terms the Tudor administration could process: lands, kin, maintenance, obedience and service. That translation gave her a route into power, but it also forced her authority into the state's categories.
pages.detail: The petition is not transparent autobiography. It is an act designed to produce an answer.

pages.title: Go from the bay; come into the court world
pages.body: Téigh means go; tar means come. From Clew Bay, Gráinne had to téigh go Londain — go to London. From the court's point of view, she had to tar into its process: arrive, answer questions and make her case on paper.
pages.detail: The paired verbs keep perspective visible. The journey is both movement away from home and arrival into somebody else's system.

pages.title: The crossing is an absence in the record
pages.body: The papers prove the London process, not a day-by-day voyage. We can follow the geographic fact of leaving the Mayo coast and reaching the machinery around Elizabeth's court. We cannot supply weather, companions' dialogue or a cinematic audience scene simply because the journey invites them.
pages.detail: Restraint keeps the real decision visible: she left the system she knew because it could no longer protect her.

pages.title: Arrival meant questions, not a recovered conversation
pages.body: The surviving trail places her in the Queen's process and leads to eighteen written questions associated with Burghley. Later storytelling richly furnishes a meeting at Greenwich. The production story stays with what the papers can carry: arrival, questioning and an answer pursued through administration.
pages.detail: The audience tradition belongs in afterlife, not as dialogue inserted here.

pages.title: Her name would now be held on paper
pages.body: The crossing brought Gráinne into a process that needed names, relationships, lands and claims in writing. That could constrain her, but it also created the surviving documentary encounter at the centre of this story. The next chapter begins where the questions place her name.
pages.detail: The record is not neutral access to a private self. It is the form in which her case could be heard.

chapters.title: Gráinne sa Taifead · Gráinne in the record

pages.title: Eighteen questions begin with a name
pages.body: Ainm means name. The published calendar places “Grany Ne Malley” at the head of eighteen questions. Mise means me or I in the emphatic form. The earlier motion word tar — come — reaches its documentary payoff here: her name has come into the record. Find that name, then answer with a name in your own voice.
pages.detail: The compact manuscript form still awaits diplomatic transcription; the calendar rendering remains the approved learner-facing form.
pages.visualCaption: The National Archives · SP 63/170 f. 201 · educational-use posture under D19

pages.title: The state fixes her into its own spelling
pages.body: The anglicised heading is not the name she would have written in modern Irish. It is the form the English administrative record preserves. Finding it matters because the document turns a remembered figure into a trace that can be inspected, cited and questioned.
pages.detail: The interface may highlight the name on the real folio, but it must not alter the source image or imply the calendar spelling is a preferred Irish form.
pages.visualCaption: Source image with live interface highlighting · not an edited facsimile

pages.title: The archive preserves one side of the encounter
pages.context: English administration · silence in the Irish annals
pages.body: Gráinne does not appear in the surviving Irish annals. Most of the written record used here comes from English administration: petitions, questions, answers and official correspondence made for government business. That record is substantial, but its survival gives the state unusual power over what can now be told.
pages.detail: Absence from the annals does not make the administrative papers false or complete. It tells us to read their evidence together with the purposes that produced and preserved it.

pages.title: The answers recover relationships and claims
pages.body: The answers name her father, marriages, children, lands and the ways she said she had maintained herself and her people. The teaghlach introduced around Clew Bay now reappears in a document built to measure political connection.
pages.detail: Family returns here because the source names it, not because the chapter needs a vocabulary review.

pages.title: Her voice survives inside another power's questions
pages.body: The answers matter because they carry claims made in her name. They are also constrained by what Burghley asked and by what might persuade the Queen's administration. Calling them either pure voice or pure imposition would lose the encounter. They are both testimony and political instrument.
pages.detail: This is the evidence boundary the learner should carry forward into the royal reply.

pages.title: A written case now demanded a written answer
pages.body: By answering the articles, Gráinne made the administration hold her name, family and claims in a form it could not simply treat as coastal rumour. The next question is narrower and harder: what would the Queen's answer on paper actually change in Mayo?
pages.detail: The chapter ends with administrative leverage, not a recovered private audience.

chapters.title: An Freagra Ríoga · The royal answer
chapters.place: 6 September 1593 · the order and its limits

pages.title: The Queen's administration answered
pages.body: Freagair means answer. A draft dated 6 September 1593 instructed Bingham concerning Gráinne and named members of her family. It is the source for the royal response. The manuscript image the learner handled belongs to July; this September draft is supported through transcription and calendar evidence.
pages.detail: Keeping the two documents distinct prevents the source encounter from becoming a composite that never existed.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of a Tudor presence chamber · not a documentary interior

pages.title: The order said to give relief
pages.body: Tabhair means give. The response directed that imprisoned kin be released and that Gráinne receive maintenance connected to her sons' estates while living peaceably. On paper, the state moved from hearing the request to ordering relief.
pages.detail: The wording must remain tied to the reviewed transcription. The chapter does not turn an instruction into proof that every term took effect.

pages.title: The response names the family stakes
pages.context: Sons and brother in the royal draft
pages.body: The draft names Gráinne's sons and her brother Donal in the business sent to Bingham. The family words learned around Clew Bay now appear as administrative terms: people whose release, estates and treatment the order addresses.
pages.detail: The paper's naming is practical and political. It is not evidence that the court understood the family as Gráinne did.

pages.title: An order was not the same as an outcome
pages.body: The draft created leverage, but Bingham still controlled implementation on the coast. What Gráinne had asked for could be acknowledged in London and still be delayed, narrowed or resisted in Connacht. The danger of caill — loss — did not vanish when the letter was written.
pages.detail: This distinction is the chapter's main historical change: an answer exists, but preservation remains partial.

pages.body: Choose the conclusion the evidence supports.

pages.title: Bingham did not hurry to yield
pages.body: Bingham resisted giving the order full effect. The paper therefore changed the argument without ending the struggle: Gráinne could point to royal instruction, while the governor could still obstruct what happened locally.
pages.detail: The conflict is administrative and material at once. That is why the story cannot end in London.

pages.title: Preservation remained unfinished
pages.body: Gráinne had made the state answer her in writing and had won a measure of protection for herself and named kin. Yet by 1595 she was pressing again. The royal answer preserved possibility, not a settled ending. The final chapter returns to the coast with that unfinished action.
pages.detail: The voyage chart begins its return line here, but does not close it.

chapters.title: Ar Ais chun an Chósta · Return and afterlife
chapters.place: Clew Bay · Rockfleet · the coast today

pages.title: The answer did not end the asking
pages.body: Arís means again. By 1595 Gráinne was pressing her case again, evidence that the 1593 order had not resolved the struggle. The earlier motion word téigh now meets arís, but the record does not require us to invent another journey. Iarr arís — ask again — is the documented final action: persistence after a partial answer.
pages.detail: The later pressure is condensed here so the ending stays on unresolved preservation rather than opening another administrative timeline.

pages.title: The coast still holds the places
pages.body: Cósta means coast. Clew Bay, its islands and Rockfleet still occupy the same western edge, though the sixteenth-century political world is gone. The farraige, bá, áit and caisleán from the opening chapters can be located again here, in the present.
pages.detail: Place is continuity, not proof that every later story happened exactly as told.

pages.context: Tá an caisleán ar an gcósta

pages.title: The record and the later stories do different work
pages.body: Later stories picture Gráinne refusing to bow, carrying a dagger or speaking with Elizabeth in Latin. Those tales express the defiance people wanted to remember. The documents preserve a different act: she crossed into English power, answered its questions and made it answer her.
pages.detail: The afterlife is presented affirmatively as reception, never smuggled back into the 1593 record as eyewitness fact.

pages.title: Her last years remain a softer edge
pages.context: Later galley reports · death date uncertain
pages.body: Later evidence continues to associate her with a Connacht galley into the early seventeenth century. A death around 1603 is often given, but the exact date and place are not firm enough to bear a dramatic final scene. The coast, the papers and the afterlife outlast that uncertainty.
pages.detail: The story closes without manufacturing a deathbed or a final voyage the sources do not provide.

pages.title: The voyage chart now carries both directions
pages.body: The chart joins the bay outline, kin marks, Rockfleet, fleet routes, the broken local path, the road to London, the ainm — name — in the record and the incomplete return. It carries Is mise beside the documentary name, and keeps iarr, freagair and tabhair distinct: asking, answering and giving did not have the same effect. It is a learner-made account of the journey through the evidence, not a replica of a historical chart.
pages.detail: Story mode may complete the account and open the route. Learning mode still requires its final retrieval before Mayo can turn gold.

pages.title: What remains is a name, a coast and an unfinished answer
pages.body: Gráinne did not secure a clean victory, and Bingham did not erase her authority or her case. The surviving papers hold a woman forcing herself and her family into the state's attention; the Mayo coast keeps the places that made that action possible. Record and legend now stand beside one another without becoming the same thing.
pages.detail: The county draft is structurally complete. Gold and external testing remain behind the open specialist, audio, rights, accessibility and device gates.
